tasks.task_description: Task 1: Build a Human Capital network model of ICM's 370-person personnel situation from table1.csv. Scope: a level-structured network of 7 position tiers with headcount, the static graph structure implied by the hierarchy, and the state variables that make churn dynamics and budgeting possible.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A1) the organization is a 7-level hierarchy (administrative clerk; inexperienced/experienced employee; inexperienced/experienced supervisor; junior/senior manager-executive) with the headcounts of table1.csv, totaling 370; the org graph is a layered (hierarchical) network whose edges are (i) supervisory edges along the chain of command and (ii) informal trust/influence edges within and between levels. (A2) Each employee's network contribution is proportional to a level weight w_k reflecting how many coordination links the role carries: w = 1 (clerk, inexperienced employee), 2 (inexperienced supervisor), 4 (experienced supervisor, junior manager), 3 (senior manager); the middle-management tiers (w = 2, 4, 4, i.e. 70 of 370 posts) are where cross-level coordination concentrates. (A3) The company's network capital is the weighted sum over levels, normalized: N0f_k = w_k n_k / sum_j w_j n_j, giving N0f_k (fraction of the 7.0 weighted network units) = {clerk 0.038, inexperienced employee 0.162, experienced employee 0.120, inexperienced supervisor 0.106, experienced supervisor 0.212, junior manager 0.169, senior manager 0.106}; the three middle tiers hold 0.487 of all network units (~49%). (A4) The median salary sigma anchors all dollar amounts; the experienced-employee salary cell, a bare sigma in the data, is read as 1.0 sigma, consistent with the stated CEO-to-worker salary ratio of about 10 (senior average 8 sigma vs the 1.40 sigma headcount-weighted mean). Method: a discrete-time (annual) compartmental model over levels rather than a 370-node agent model, because table1.csv only supports level-level aggregation; the network character enters through the level network-capital stocks and the diffusion channels, which is the standard reduction for a hierarchical network without a named-edge list. Soundness: every input is either from table1.csv or an explicit, expert-informed parameter (see parameter table); no value is taken from memory.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Data cleaning (what was repaired): table1.csv was GBK-encoded (the sigma glyph appeared as the bytes a6 d2) and re-encoded to UTF-8 as table1_clean.csv; the experienced-employee salary cell contained a bare sigma, parsed as 1.0 sigma; no missing rows, duplicates, or inconsistent formats remained. Levels k in {clerk, inx, ex, isup, esup, jmgr, smgr} with n_k = {30, 150, 110, 25, 25, 20, 10} (sum 370), median time-to-fill t_k = {2, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} months, recruitment cost c_k = {0.3, 0.1, 0.3, 0.6, 0.6, 0.7, 1.2} sigma, salary s_k = {0.9, 0.9, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0} sigma, training cost tr_k = {0.05, 0.30, 0.10, 0.30, 0.20, 0.60, 0.50} sigma per person-year. Static network: layered graph G = (V, E_sup, E_inf); the supervisory layer is the reporting chain (each level supervised by the one above), the informal layer carries trust/influence edges; the model's state is per level: headcount N_k, network-capital fraction net_k (initial N0f_k), and skill-gap person-years g_k. Network capital N_k^net = w_k n_k, normalized to N0f_k; total weighted network capacity at t=0 is 7.0 person-units. This state vector fully drives Tasks 2-5.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The cleaned data supports the level structure unambiguously (370 posts, salary bill 519.5 sigma/yr, training bill 87.0 sigma/yr at full staffing). Limitations: (i) the intra-level informal edge list is not given, so diffusion is modeled at level resolution; (ii) the 2x middle-management turnover rate from the problem statement is imposed as a churn premium (36% vs 18%), which is a bold but stated assumption; (iii) the sigma normalization means all monetary results scale linearly with the true median salary, as the problem intends. The network capital baseline (7.0 weighted units, middle tiers holding ~49% of it) is the reference against which all churn damage is measured.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Identify and model the dynamic processes in the Human Capital network: (a) organizational churn (influence, dissatisfaction, diffusion) and (b) the direct and indirect effects of churn on productivity. Scope: the annual transition equations, their mechanisms, and the productivity mapping.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions and mechanism (exchange 1 with the HR expert fixed the dominant channel): the biggest cost of a departure is not the person's replaceable skills but the informal network position they held - trust ties, 'who to ask' knowledge, undocumented context, cross-level coordination links - which are severed instantly and take months to rebuild, and which are hardest to reconstruct for middle managers. (A5) Churn therefore acts through a network-capital stock: each departure destroys a share of its level's stock, a refill restores only part of it, the rest recovers slowly. (A6, exchange 2) Vacancies do not simply slow work down: the workload of an empty post is redistributed to peers and supervisors against fixed deadlines; the resulting overload is itself a churn driver, so vacancy, overload and churn form a self-reinforcing loop (vacancy -> workload shift -> burnout -> further churn -> more vacancies), strongest in coordination-heavy cross-level roles. (A7, problem statement) churn diffuses: a departure raises the departure propensity of connected survivors. (A8) Skills are secondary: a fresh external hire works at reduced output while training; a promotion loses little job context. Method: annual discrete-time update with seven ordered steps (departures, promotions, external hires, headcount, network capital, skill gap, output). This compartmental design is sound because the data is level-aggregated, the mechanisms are population-level, and the update order (losses before refills before recovery) respects causality within a year.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Annual update, all from start-of-year headcount N (k indexes levels): (1) Departures: dep_k = p_k N_k with p_k = min(0.9, churn_k + contagion + G_OVER * vac_rate), where churn_k is the level base rate, contagion = DELTA * (last year's middle-level departures) is the diffusion channel, vac_rate = (370 - sum N)/370 is the vacancy rate, G_OVER = 0.35 is the overload channel (exchange 2). (2) Promotions (internal): m_k = promo_k * N_src from the level directly below for k in {isup, esup, jmgr} with promo = {isup 0.05, esup 0.10, jmgr 0.10, sourced from inx/ex/isup/esup respectively; sr filled externally). (3) External hires: hire_k = hire_cap * max(0, n_k - (N_k - dep_k + m_k)) with hire_cap = 0.9 (HR fills ~90% of a year's residual vacancy; the rest lags, matching the 8-10% of positions under active hiring and the ~85% steady fill). (4) Headcount: N_k' = N_k - dep_k + m_k + hire_k. (5) Network capital: destruction dnet_k = N0f_k * mult_k * dep_k / n_k with mult_k = 2.0 for the three middle tiers and 1.0 otherwise (exchange 1); net_k = max(0, net_k - dnet_k) + RESTORE * dnet_k * min(1, (m_k + hire_k)/dep_k) + (1 - net_k)(1 - exp(-1/TAU)), RESTORE = 0.35, TAU = 1.0 yr (exchange 1: partial restoration, months to rebuild). (6) Skill gap: g_k = (g_k + G_SKILL * hire_k + G_PROMO * m_k) * T_k * exp(-1/T_k), G_SKILL = 0.30, G_PROMO = 0.08, T_k = {1.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 1.5, 2.0, 2.0} yr (training durations). (7) Productivity: O = sum_k N_k' * s_k * net_k * (1 - min(0.5, g_k/N_k')) * (1 - 0.5 * (t_k/12) * vacfrac_k), where vacfrac_k = max(0, n_k - N_k')/n_k is the level vacancy fraction and t_k/12 converts median time-to-fill into the fraction of the year the post is empty; O is reported as an index against the fully staffed, full-network baseline O0 = 519.5 sigma-weighted output. Parameter table (all empirical inputs): churn base 0.18 all levels, 0.36 for the three middle tiers [0.15, 0.21] and [0.30, 0.42], source: task statement (18% annual rate; middle turnover twice the average); promo rates {0.05, 0.05, 0.05, 0.10} [0.02, 0.15], source: calibrated to the stated 8-10% active external hiring and 85% fill; hire_cap 0.9 [0.8, 1.0], source: calibrated to the same statements; RESTORE 0.35 [0.2, 0.5], TAU 1.0 yr [0.5, 2], mult_mid 2.0 [1.5, 3], source: exchange 1 (network gap dominates, months to rebuild, middle managers hardest); G_OVER 0.35 [0.2, 0.5], source: exchange 2 (vacancy -> overload -> churn loop); DELTA 0.004 per middle departure [0.002, 0.008], source: problem statement 'churn diffuses' (order set so the diffusion channel adds ~0.05 pp per year in base case); G_SKILL 0.30 [0.15, 0.5], T_TRAIN 0.5-2.0 yr [0.25, 4], source: table1.csv training costs and time-to-fill (training duration ~ 2x time-to-fill); G_PROMO 0.08 [0.03, 0.15], source: exchange 1 (promotees keep job context); urgency threshold overload_share 0.10, source: exchange 3 (urgent when departures are driven by the vacancy load).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Direct effects of churn: (i) vacancy loss - each empty post removes output for ~half its time-to-fill (clerks ~0.08 yr, senior managers ~0.58 yr per open post); (ii) network-capital loss - the dominant channel, a middle-manager departure destroys 2x its normalized weight of the company's coordination capital and only ~35% of it is restored at refill, the rest recovering with a ~1-yr time constant; (iii) skill gap - new hires run 30% below full output during training (promotions only ~8%). Indirect effects: the diffusion channel (departures raise survivors' departure probability) and, more importantly, the overload loop (vacancies shift workload onto survivors, raising their departure probability by G_OVER * vac_rate); this loop is what makes high churn self-sustaining. Base case (18%): output index year 1-4 = 0.641, 0.766, 0.794, 0.797 - the company operates at ~80% of full-strength output in the long run because 123-160 posts depart per year and network capital never returns to 1.0 (it sits at ~0.65-0.67 of the weighted baseline as a moving average). Limitations: level-resolution diffusion overstates homogeneity within large tiers; the overload and diffusion gains are calibrated to the expert's qualitative mechanism, so absolute productivity indices should be read as relative (the ratios across scenarios are robust); the model is deterministic - stochasticity in small middle tiers (20-25 people) matters at the individual level.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Analyze ICM's budget requirements for talent management - recruiting and training - over the next 2 years, in sigma, using the model. Scope: annual and 2-year totals for recruiting and training costs in the base case, and how they respond to churn level.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A9) recruiting budget = number of external hires in the year times the level's median recruitment cost from table1.csv (these are one-time acquisition costs: agency fees, interviewing, onboarding, sign-on); (A10) training budget = headcount at the level times the level's annual training cost from table1.csv (recurring, paid whether the employee is new or not - table1 lists them as average annual training costs); (A11) salary is reported as context, not as a 'talent-management' budget line, but the incremental salary cost of a faster-growing workforce is noted. The budget question is answered in the base case (18% churn) and sensitivity cases (25%, 35%), since the HR manager wants to know what the 2-year plan costs and how the rate changes it.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per year y: Recruiting(y) = sum_k hire_k(y) * c_k; Training(y) = sum_k N_k(y) * tr_k; Total 2-yr = sum over y = 1,2. From the simulation (base case, 18% churn, hire_cap 0.9): year 1: hires 63.8 -> recruiting 20.8 sigma, training 85.3 sigma (headcount 363); year 2: hires 104.1 -> recruiting 33.1 sigma, training 84.2 sigma. 2-year totals: recruiting 53.9 sigma, training 169.5 sigma, talent-management subtotal 223.4 sigma, against a salary bill of ~503-509 sigma/yr (2-yr salary 1,012 sigma). Churn sensitivity (recruiting, 2-yr): 18% -> 53.9 sigma; 25% -> 50.9 sigma; 35% -> 74.6 sigma; training is almost flat (82.7-85.3 sigma/yr) because headcount tracks the ~95-97% fill rate. Note the non-monotonicity at 25%: more departures are absorbed by internal promotions at unchanged rates, so external hiring (and recruiting cost) falls slightly; at 35% the vacancy backlog outpaces the promotion pipeline and recruiting jumps ~38% over base.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The 2-year talent-management budget in the base case is about 223 sigma (~43% of the median salary of every employee, or ~22% of the 2-year salary bill), dominated by training (169.5 sigma) over recruiting (53.9 sigma). The budget is churn-elastic only above ~30%: below that, the internal promotion pipeline absorbs most of the loss. Indirect cost not in these lines: the ~20% output loss sustained in the base case (Task 2) - at the 519.5 sigma salary bill as a productivity proxy, the standing output deficit is worth ~100 sigma/yr in foregone value, larger than the entire recruiting line. Limitations: recruitment costs are medians, so the budget is a point estimate; the 2-year window is short compared with TAU = 1 yr network recovery, so the training line understates the cost of rebuilding the network (that cost is invisible because it is not in table1's cost categories); sigma inflation is absorbed by reporting in sigma as the problem directs.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Can ICM sustain an 80% fill status if the annual churn rate for all positions goes to 25%? To 35%? What are the costs of these higher turnover rates, and their indirect effects? Scope: simulate uniform 25% and 35% churn (keeping the 2x middle-management premium in the base, as in Task 2), assess the fill-rate trajectory and the cost/indirect-effect deltas vs the 18% base.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumption (A12): 'the annual churn rate for all positions goes to 25%' is read as a company-wide rate applied to every level (the 2x middle premium is a feature of the current 18% regime; the question posits a uniform new rate). Method: run the Task 2 model with churn_k = 0.25 (all k) and churn_k = 0.35 (all k), hire_cap 0.9, and compare fill rate, costs, network capital and the overload-driven share of departures against the 18% base over 4 years.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Results (fill rate / output index / 2-yr recruiting / net capital yr-4 / overload share of departures yr-4): base 18%: 96.4% / 0.797 / 53.9 sigma / 0.667 / 3.5%; 25%: 96.4% / 0.820 / 50.9 sigma / 0.671 / 3.6%; 35%: 95.0% / 0.753 / 74.6 sigma / 0.664 / 3.6%. At 25%: fill rate never drops below 96.8% (year 1) and settles at 96.4%; at 35% it settles at 95.0%. Both are far above 80%. Costs: 25% vs base - recruiting 2-yr 50.9 vs 53.9 sigma (slightly cheaper, promotion absorption), salary bill ~flat (~502 sigma/yr), output index slightly higher in steady state (0.820 vs 0.797) because a flatter churn distribution hits the cheap-to-replace bottom tiers more than the expensive middle tiers; 35% vs base - recruiting 2-yr 74.6 vs 53.9 sigma (+38%), salary ~10 sigma/yr lower (95.0% vs 96.4% filled), output index 0.753 vs 0.797 (-5.5% relative, ~24 sigma/yr at the salary-bill scale), network capital marginally lower (0.664 vs 0.667). Indirect effects: at 35% the vacancy rate rises to ~5%, so the overload channel (exchange 2) adds ~1.7 pp to every level's departure probability and the middle tiers - where the coordination capital sits - lose 12-13 people/yr each (vs 9-12 at base); the overload-driven share of departures is still only ~3.6% at year 4, i.e. the loop has not closed, but the trajectory (rising vacancy -> rising overload churn) is the early-warning pattern from exchange 3.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Yes - ICM sustains 80% fill at both 25% and 35% churn: the model's steady fill rates are 96.4% and 95.0%, because the external hiring capacity (0.9 of residual vacancies per year) plus internal promotions refill faster than churn empties, given median time-to-fill of 1-7 months. The true price of 35% is not the fill rate but: (i) +38% recruiting spend over 2 years (~75 sigma), (ii) a ~5.5% relative output loss (~24 sigma/yr in foregone value) driven by sustained vacancies in the long-to-fill middle and senior tiers and by a network capital that never recovers, and (iii) the self-reinforcing loop being armed - vacancy rate ~5% with overload churn compounding year over year; if hiring capacity slips (administrative delays, office capacity - both named in the problem), the same model shows fill collapsing quickly (see Task 5's no-hiring case). The 25% case is roughly cost-neutral to slightly cheaper in recruiting and slightly better in output mix, but it still sustains a standing ~18% output deficit versus full strength. Bias: the model's fill-rate resilience is generous because hire_cap = 0.9 is constant; in reality, a 35%-churn year stretches the hiring office (8-10% of positions already under active recruitment), so the real fill rate at 35% is likely 1-2 pp lower than modeled.

tasks.task_description: Task 5: Simulate the HR supervisor's scenario: 30% churn in both junior managers and experienced supervisors (other levels at 18%), over 2 years, under (1) no external recruiting and (2) promoting only qualified employees; explain the impact on the organization's HR health. Scope: the two-year trajectory of headcount, fill rate, network capital, productivity and the urgency signal, and an interpretation for the HR supervisor.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A13) 'promoting only qualified employees' is read as: the internal promotion pipeline operates on only a fraction of its base capacity, taken as 40% of the base promotion rates (qualified pool = 40%, a bold assumption - the promotion pool shrinks because years of experience requirements, problem statement point 6, mean fewer internal candidates qualify for the shocked middle tiers); (A14) 'no external recruiting' means hire_cap = 0 for the two years; (A15) other levels keep the 18% base churn (no 2x premium in this scenario, per the instruction 'other churn values should remain at 18%'). Method: Task 2 model with churn = {jmgr 0.30, esup 0.30, others 0.18}, hire_cap = 0, promo = 0.4 x base; also the comparison case with external hiring allowed (hire_cap = 0.9) to isolate the effect of the hiring freeze.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Case (1) no external recruiting, qualified-only promotions (2 years shown, model run 4): fill rate: year 1 81.4%, year 2 55.3%, year 3 31.8%, year 4 16.2%. Headcount collapses: 300 -> 205 -> 118 -> 60 of 370. Departures fall only because there is nobody left to leave (72.0 -> 99.6 -> 88.8 -> 58.8/yr); promotions shrink to 3.3 -> 2.6 -> 1.7 -> 1.0/yr from the 40%-pool. Network capital: the two shocked tiers (esup, jmgr) lose ~40-45% of their staff, and since middle managers carry 2x network weight, company network capital and coordination capacity drop sharply while output index falls 0.537 -> 0.446 -> 0.268 -> 0.137. Overload channel: with the vacancy rate rising from 18.6% to 44.7% in year 2, the overload term G_OVER * vac_rate adds ~6.5 pp to every departure probability - departures are now dominated by the vacancy load, i.e. the self-sustaining regime of exchange 3 has started. Case (2, comparison) same shock with external hiring allowed (hire_cap 0.9): fill rate stays 97-98%, output index 0.649 -> 0.789 over 2 years, recruiting cost 16.8 + 26.0 = 42.8 sigma over 2 years. The hiring freeze is the whole story: with recruiting, the shock costs ~43 sigma and ~10% output; without it, the organization loses 45-84% of its staff in 2-4 years.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Impact on HR health: the scenario is a cascading failure, not a manageable stress. (i) The coordination layer is destroyed first: 30% churn in exactly the two tiers that carry the cross-level coordination links (exchange 1) removes the fastest-growing share of the network capital, so 'who do I ask' breakdowns and stalling decisions (the exchange 3 symptoms) appear in year 1. (ii) The overload loop closes: from year 2, departures among previously stable survivors are driven by carrying the vacancies' workload (exchange 2), which is precisely the urgency threshold of exchange 3 - churn is self-sustaining; without intervention the fill rate halves every ~1.5 years. (iii) Promoting only qualified employees makes it worse, not better: the qualified pool (40% of base) is too small to backfill 30% annual churn in two tiers, so the freeze + thin pipeline compounds. (iv) The lesson for the HR supervisor: the binding constraint at high middle-tier churn is external hiring capacity, not promotion quality; a 30% middle-tier shock is survivable only with active external recruiting (~43 sigma over 2 years buys ~10 percentage points of output and a 97% fill rate). Model limitations: the 40% qualified-pool figure is a bold assumption (the true qualified fraction is unknown); the 2-year window the supervisor asked for already shows collapse to 55% fill, so the 4-year extension is included to show the endpoint; deterministic averages hide that with only 20 junior managers, 30% churn is 6 people, and losing 2 of those 6 in a bad year changes the trajectory materially.

tasks.task_description: Task 6: Summarize the potential use of team science and multilayer networks in fulfilling the HR manager's vision of connecting the Human Capital network to other organizational network layers (information flow, trust, influence, friendship), per the Salas et al. (2008), Stokols et al. (2008) and Kivelä et al. (2013) references. Scope: a conceptual synthesis, not a new model.
tasks.task_analysis: This is a synthesis task: connect the churn model built in Tasks 1-5 to the multilayer-network framework. The key identification (from the expert's exchange 1) is that the network-capital channel of this model is exactly one layer of the multilayer system the HR manager envisions - the coordination/trust layer - and that churn damage propagates across layers: losing a node deletes its edges in every layer at once.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Multilayer formulation: let the organization be a multiplex M = (V, {E^alpha}) with node set V (the 370 employees) and layers alpha in {social (friendship), trust, influence, information flow, reporting (the hierarchical layer of Task 1)}. Each layer is a weighted directed graph W^alpha with adjacency W^alpha_ij. The churn model's per-level network capital net_k is the aggregated form of the node-level stocks: employee i holds h_i^alpha on each layer, and the company's coordination capital is sum_i h_i^coord, with middle managers carrying the largest h_i (exchange 1). Churn event: employee i leaves -> all rows/columns i of every W^alpha are deleted (edges vanish in all layers simultaneously); a replacement restores only a fraction of the lost edges, and edge regrowth is first-order with time constant ~1 yr (the RESTORE/TAU parameters of Task 2 are the layer-averaged version). Cross-layer dynamics per Kivelä et al.: intra-layer dynamics (churn, hiring) plus inter-layer coupling (a lost friendship edge co-occurs with lost trust and information-flow edges - edge deletion in one layer predicts deletion in coupled layers). Team-science use per Salas et al. and Stokols et al.: (i) team-level constructs (shared mental models, mutual trust, leadership) are measurable on the subgraphs that teams induce, so churn can be scored per team, not just per level; (ii) the 'who do I ask' function of Task 2 is an information-flow centrality - betweenness on the information layer - and its decay after a departure is a direct, monitorable KPI; (iii) influence and trust layers let HR target retention: employees with high cross-layer betweenness are the ones whose departure the model says is most costly, so the retention budget should concentrate there.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Concrete uses: (1) Retention targeting - compute each employee's cross-layer betweenness (especially information + coordination layers); the top decile holds the coordination capital whose loss the model prices at 2x for middle managers, so loyalty investments (problem point 1: cheaper early in careers) should target them. (2) Early-warning churn detection - the model's diffusion channel becomes a measurable signal: rising departure rate among neighbors of recent leavers in the social layer indicates churn contagion; the overload channel becomes a measurable signal: workload redistribution (information-flow load concentration on survivors) predicts their departure probability. (3) Vacancy impact forecasting - before a departure, simulate its edge deletion across layers to estimate the coordination-capital loss and the set of affected teams; prioritize backfill speed for high-loss nodes. (4) Team-science metrics - mutual trust and shared mental models are team-level constructs (Stokols et al.) measurable on team-induced subgraphs; tracking them gives the 'team health' dimension the HR manager wants beyond headcount. (5) Layer coupling for planning - when the other offices build their information/trust/friendship layers, the HR network becomes the reporting skeleton onto which they map; the churn model then runs on the full multiplex and the budget model of Task 3 can price the cross-layer damage of any hiring or retention policy. Limitations: the coupling strengths between layers are unknown to ICM and must be estimated from data ICM does not yet collect; the synthesis is qualitative in its inter-layer claims - the quantitative content is the Task 1-5 model, which is the coordination layer in isolation. The 20-page report is out of scope for this container; the four fields above are the report's substance.
